paragraphs: Finding a solution to a combinatorial problem and estimating how many solutions exist are different challenges. Learned neural solvers have made progress on the first, while counting has remained largely dependent on manually designed methods. This paper introduces belief propagation neural networks, or BPNNs, to bring learned computation into that counting setting.

BPNNs operate on factor graphs and extend belief propagation, an established iterative inference procedure. Their most constrained form, BPNN-D, preserves many desirable properties of belief propagation regardless of the learned parameter values. This gives learning room to improve the procedure while retaining a specified set of mathematical guarantees.

In experiments on Ising models, trained BPNN-D converges 1.7 times faster than ordinary belief propagation and produces tighter bounds. On challenging model-counting problems, BPNNs deliver estimates hundreds of times faster than leading handcrafted methods, with comparable estimate quality. These findings support combining an established inference structure with trainable updates: learning improves the reported computational performance without discarding all of the original method’s theoretical structure.
neurips-2020-belief-propagation-neural-n.tldr: Belief propagation neural networks learn faster counting and inference procedures while preserving several properties of classical belief propagation.

paragraphs: Weakly supervised semantic segmentation aims to label individual pixels while learning from labels that describe an entire image. A crucial intermediate step is producing pseudo-masks: estimated pixel annotations used to train the segmentation model. This paper addresses why those masks can have ambiguous boundaries even when the image-level classifier identifies the correct categories.

The authors attribute this problem to confounding context. A classifier may recognize horse and person partly through their frequent appearance together, making it difficult to determine which pixels support each category. They introduce a structural causal model that represents relationships among images, contexts, and class labels, providing a basis for analyzing this ambiguity.

Their method, Context Adjustment, or CONTA, uses that framework to remove contextual confounding bias from image-level classification and generate better pseudo-masks. Those masks then supervise the subsequent segmentation model. Experiments on PASCAL VOC 2012 and MS-COCO show improvements across several popular weakly supervised segmentation methods, reaching new state-of-the-art results. The contribution connects the quality of pixel supervision to how the upstream classifier handles contextual relationships.
neurips-2020-causal-intervention-for-wea.tldr: CONTA uses a causal model of contextual bias to improve pixel-level pseudo-masks learned from image-level labels.

paragraphs: A collection of linked documents contains information both in its text and in the connections between documents. Relational topic models analyze those sources together, but a single layer of hidden representations can limit what they express. This paper develops a hierarchical probabilistic approach intended to capture richer relationships within such document networks.

The starting point is graph Poisson factor analysis, which models interconnected documents and supplies closed-form Gibbs sampling updates. The authors then extend it into a graph Poisson gamma belief network, introducing a hierarchy of latent document representations. This progression moves from a basic relational model toward a deeper representation of document content and connectivity.

To make inference efficient and aggregate network information, the paper also introduces two variational graph autoencoders based on Weibull distributions. Experiments show that the resulting models extract high-quality hierarchical representations and improve performance over baselines on several graph analysis tasks. The stated benefit is therefore practical as well as representational: jointly modeling links and content through a hierarchy yields useful features for downstream graph analysis.
neurips-2020-deep-relational-topic-model.tldr: A hierarchical probabilistic topic model combines document content and links to learn representations that improve graph analysis tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies selecting a feasible set to maximize a nonnegative submodular objective under a matroid constraint. Submodularity expresses diminishing returns, while non-monotonicity allows adding an element to reduce the objective. The goal is a fast deterministic algorithm with a guaranteed fraction of the best feasible value, without relying on random choices.

The central idea is to build two candidate sets simultaneously through greedy search. This framework yields a one-quarter approximation in O(nr) time, improving both the guarantee and runtime of the previous deterministic result. Its faster variant, TwinGreedyFast, achieves a one-quarter-minus-epsilon guarantee in O((n/epsilon) log(r/epsilon)) time, trading a small amount of approximation quality for nearly linear scaling.

The framework also covers p-set system constraints, where TwinGreedyFast guarantees a fraction of 1/(2p+2) minus epsilon with the same runtime expression. Experiments on two network applications report better performance than the compared efficiently implemented deterministic and randomized algorithms. Those empirical findings complement the worst-case guarantees: the method offers both a provable floor on solution quality and favorable results in the tested applications.
neurips-2020-deterministic-approximation.tldr: Building two greedy candidate sets yields faster deterministic approximation algorithms for constrained non-monotone submodular maximization.

paragraphs: Sparse deep learning seeks to reduce neural-network storage and recover sparse structure in the function being learned. The paper addresses a gap between methods that work well empirically but lack theoretical support and theoretical approaches that are computationally impractical. Its objective is to combine efficient training with a statistical justification for the resulting estimates.

The authors use a fully Bayesian model with spike-and-slab priors, which represent a distinction between inactive and active components. They develop efficient variational inference procedures by continuously relaxing Bernoulli variables. This relaxation makes the discrete selection aspect more amenable to computation while maintaining a Bayesian treatment of the sparse network.

The theoretical result gives a contraction rate for the variational posterior, supporting the consistency of the proposed method. Empirically, the procedure also supplies uncertainty estimates through its predictive distribution and demonstrates consistent variable selection using a sparse multilayer network. The contribution therefore links several goals: compact models, recovery of relevant inputs, and uncertainty-aware predictions, alongside an explicit theoretical analysis of the approximation.
neurips-2020-efficient-variational-infer.tldr: Continuous relaxations make Bayesian sparse-network inference efficient while supporting consistency guarantees and empirical uncertainty estimation.

paragraphs: In large image datasets, an image can have many applicable labels, yet only a small portion may be annotated. The abstract notes that fewer than one percent of labels are annotated across all images in benchmarks such as OpenImages and LVIS. Standard training ignores these unannotated entries, leaving potentially useful supervision unused.

The paper proposes extracting additional learning signals from relationships among images and labels. Rather than treating the available annotations as the full extent of useful evidence, the approach exploits weakly supervised visual patterns to learn from unannotated labels. This addresses the central difficulty of partial annotation: the dataset contains more visual information than its explicit labels directly expose.

The authors evaluate the approach across CIFAR100, MS-COCO panoptic segmentation, OpenImage, and LVIS. They report that it can outperform baselines by margins of 2–10% on mean average precision and mean F1 across the evaluated datasets. These findings support using relationships within partially annotated data to strengthen training, making the existing annotation effort more useful for multi-label visual recognition.
neurips-2020-exploiting-weakly-supervise.tldr: Relationships among images and labels provide additional supervision that improves learning from partially annotated visual datasets.

paragraphs: FixMatch addresses image classification when only a small number of images have labels and many others are unlabeled. Its contribution is a simple way to turn selected predictions on unlabeled images into training targets. The method combines confidence-based selection with a requirement that predictions remain consistent across differently augmented versions of an image.

First, the model predicts a label for a weakly augmented unlabeled image. It keeps that prediction as a pseudo-label only when confidence is high. The model then trains on a strongly augmented version of the same image, using the retained pseudo-label as its target. Confidence determines which predictions supply supervision, while augmentation creates the corresponding consistency task.

The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art results across several standard semi-supervised benchmarks. On CIFAR-10, FixMatch reaches 94.93% accuracy with 250 labels and 88.61% with 40 labels, equivalent to four per class. The authors also conduct extensive ablations to investigate which experimental factors matter most. These results show that this relatively simple training procedure can be effective under the tested conditions with very limited labeled data.
neurips-2020-fixmatch-simplifying-semi-s.tldr: FixMatch trains on confident pseudo-labels across weak and strong image augmentations, achieving strong results with very few labels.

paragraphs: Some datasets have a manifold structure: their meaningful variation lies on a lower-dimensional shape within a larger space. This paper introduces manifold-learning flows, called M-flows, that learn both that shape and a tractable probability density defined on it. The model therefore represents where the data lie and how probability is distributed along that structure.

M-flows combine aspects of normalizing flows, generative adversarial networks, autoencoders, and energy-based models. A central methodological point concerns training: the authors argue that maximum likelihood alone should not be used for these models. They instead introduce an algorithm that separates updates to the manifold from updates to the density, treating the two learning tasks distinctly.

Across a range of experiments, M-flows learn the data manifold and enable better inference than standard flows operating in the surrounding data space. The authors also identify potential uses in dimensionality reduction, denoising, and out-of-distribution detection. Those possibilities follow from the representation’s intended structure, while the stated experimental finding is improved inference and successful manifold learning in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2020-flows-for-simultaneous-mani.tldr: M-flows separately learn a data manifold and its probability density, improving inference over standard flows in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Filtering estimates a changing hidden state from observations arriving over time. In a hidden Markov model, this inference depends on an assumed observation likelihood. This paper considers what happens when that likelihood is misspecified, meaning the model’s description of observations does not adequately match the data-generating process.

The authors build filtering recursions using the loss-based perspective of generalized Bayesian inference. In particular, they use beta-divergence to obtain principled procedures designed to resist contamination in observations. This changes how observations contribute to inference, giving the framework a way to address mismatch in the observation model rather than simply applying the usual likelihood-based update.

Sequential Monte Carlo makes the framework computationally usable: standard particle methods and their convergence results can be adapted to the generalized setting. The authors demonstrate the approach on object tracking and Gaussian process regression, observing improvements over standard filtering algorithms. The contribution combines a robust inference formulation with an established computational approach, making the proposed updates practical while carrying over relevant convergence analysis.
neurips-2020-generalised-bayesian-filter.tldr: Generalized Bayesian updates and particle methods provide robust filtering under misspecified observation likelihoods.

paragraphs: Neural lossy image compression represents an image through latent variables that can be stored compactly while allowing an approximate reconstruction. Established approaches use hierarchical variational autoencoders and an inference network to predict those variables. This paper investigates how approximations in that inference process constrain compression performance, even when the underlying model architecture is already effective.

The authors identify three sources of approximation error: amortization, discretization, and marginalization gaps. They propose corresponding remedies using iterative inference, stochastic annealing for discrete optimization, and bits-back coding. Together, these changes revisit how a compressible representation is inferred and coded. The work also reports the first application of bits-back coding to lossy compression.

Experiments include extensive comparisons with baselines and ablation studies, and achieve new state-of-the-art lossy compression performance using an established VAE architecture. Only the inference method changes. This makes the result especially informative: the reported gains show that improving how a model is used to encode an image can substantially matter, alongside the usual focus on developing a different model architecture.
neurips-2020-improving-inference-for-neu.tldr: Addressing three inference approximation gaps improves lossy image compression without changing the underlying VAE architecture.

paragraphs: Manifold learning seeks to capture the geometry underlying data represented in a high-dimensional space. Many methods do this by directly producing lower-dimensional coordinates, which can be awkward to reuse in downstream applications. This paper proposes learning geometry indirectly through a heat kernel, making the learned information available in a form usable by kernel-based models.

A heat kernel describes how heat would spread across the manifold according to its heat equation. That spreading behavior contains information about the manifold’s geometry. By explicitly learning the kernel, the method implicitly learns aspects of the underlying manifold without making an explicit low-dimensional embedding its primary output. The paper provides both a practical algorithm and theoretical analysis.

The authors apply the learned kernel to data generation with deep generative models and to Bayesian inference with Stein Variational Gradient Descent. Extensive experiments report state-of-the-art results against existing methods on those two tasks. The significance is the connection between geometric representation and downstream computation: learning the kernel supplies manifold information directly in a form these methods can use.
neurips-2020-learning-manifold-implicitl.tldr: Learning a manifold’s heat kernel provides reusable geometric information that improves tested generation and Bayesian inference tasks.

paragraphs: Graphs with multiple relation types often grow as new entities appear. Those entities may initially have very few observed connections, making predictions difficult. This paper formulates few-shot out-of-graph link prediction to include both links connecting familiar and new entities and links joining two new entities, using only a few edges per new node.

The proposed Graph Extrapolation Networks, or GEN, use a transductive meta-learning framework. The system meta-learns a node embedding network for predictions involving seen and unseen nodes, together with a link prediction network for relationships between unseen nodes. A stochastic embedding layer further represents uncertainty when predicting connections between new entities with limited available evidence.

The authors evaluate GEN on multiple benchmarks for knowledge graph completion and drug-drug interaction prediction, reporting significant improvements over relevant baselines on out-of-graph tasks. The work broadens the prediction problem beyond attaching a new node to a familiar graph. It also addresses relationships within the newly arriving group, where both endpoints have sparse observations and the model must account for uncertainty.
neurips-2020-learning-to-extrapolate-kno.tldr: GEN meta-learns link prediction for sparsely connected new graph entities, including uncertain relationships between two unseen nodes.

paragraphs: Neural networks can be sensitive to input noise and adversarial perturbations. This paper takes inspiration from the Bayesian brain hypothesis, which proposes that perception uses an internal generative model to update beliefs about sensory input. The authors translate that idea into a requirement for consistency between a network’s interpretation and its generative model.

Their framework, Convolutional Neural Networks with Feedback, adds recurrent generative feedback and latent variables to existing convolutional architectures. Predictions are produced through alternating maximum a posteriori inference in a Bayesian framework. This creates an iterative process for making predictions consistent with the model’s internal generative account, extending the computation performed by a conventional feedforward network.

Experiments on standard benchmarks show considerably improved adversarial robustness over conventional feedforward convolutional networks. The result supports recurrent generative feedback as a useful architectural approach in the evaluated settings. The biological motivation supplies a design principle, while the demonstrated contribution is computational: a concrete feedback mechanism and inference procedure that improve resistance to adversarial perturbations in the reported comparisons.
neurips-2020-neural-networks-with-recurr.tldr: CNN-F adds recurrent generative feedback to convolutional networks and improves adversarial robustness in benchmark experiments.

paragraphs: Structured pruning makes a neural network smaller by deleting whole neurons or convolutional filters, but the removed computations can reduce accuracy. This paper introduces neuron merging to compensate for that lost information. The approach applies to both fully connected and convolutional layers and aims to preserve the original network’s behavior after its structure is reduced.

Neuron merging decomposes a layer’s weights into replacement weights and a scaling matrix that describes how neurons should be combined. With ReLU activations, the scaling matrix can be incorporated into the next layer under certain conditions. The authors also provide an inexpensive, data-free decomposition method based on cosine similarity between neurons.

Compared with a pruned network of the same topology, the merged network better preserves the original output feature maps and maintains accuracy without fine-tuning in the reported evaluations. For VGG-16 on CIFAR-10, the paper reports 93.16% accuracy after removing 64% of total parameters, without fine-tuning. The central contribution is thus compensation during pruning: information from removed neurons influences the surviving network through adjusted weights.
neurips-2020-neuron-merging-compensating.tldr: Neuron merging adjusts surviving weights to compensate for pruned neurons, preserving accuracy without fine-tuning in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution evaluation is intended to test whether a model generalizes when relationships between inputs and labels change. This paper examines VQA-CP, a visual question answering benchmark designed for that purpose. The authors find that common evaluation practices can reward knowledge of the benchmark’s construction, undermining what the resulting scores say about generalization.

They identify three problems. Methods often exploit explicit knowledge of how the splits were constructed, including reversing common training answers. Researchers use the out-of-distribution test set for model selection. They also assess in-domain performance after retraining on different, more balanced splits, so that assessment does not measure the same trained model’s behavior across the two settings.

The authors demonstrate the consequences with very simple methods, including a random-answer procedure that exceeds the state of the art on some question types. This is evidence of exploitable evaluation practices, rather than broad success at visual reasoning. The paper proposes short- and long-term remedies aimed at restoring the value of out-of-distribution evaluation and distinguishing benchmark-specific adaptation from the generalization the benchmark was meant to measure.
neurips-2020-on-the-value-of-out-of-dist.tldr: An analysis of VQA-CP shows how benchmark-specific strategies and evaluation practices can undermine claims of out-of-distribution generalization.

paragraphs: Image annotation becomes demanding when a person must choose the correct category from many possibilities. This paper studies a simpler interaction: the model proposes a category, and the annotator answers whether it is correct. Each response supplies one bit of information, making the annotation task a yes-or-no judgment about a specific prediction.

Learning effectively from these responses requires both accurate guesses and a way to benefit when a guess is rejected. The authors propose a multistage training procedure that incorporates negative label suppression into an existing semi-supervised learning algorithm. A rejected guess identifies a category the image does not belong to, so incorrect predictions can still contribute useful supervision.

The approach is evaluated on three popular image classification benchmarks, where the authors report greater efficiency in using a limited amount of annotation. The contribution changes both the annotation interaction and the training procedure built around it. It demonstrates a way to use partial feedback systematically, combining confirmed predictions with information from rejected labels instead of requiring a full class label for every queried image.
neurips-2020-one-bit-supervision-for-ima.tldr: One-bit supervision trains image classifiers from yes-or-no feedback on predicted labels, using both correct and rejected guesses.

paragraphs: Boosting combines weak learning rules into a stronger learner. This paper addresses the online agnostic setting, where learning proceeds sequentially and does not rely on the realizable assumption that the learning class can explain the labels perfectly. The abstract identifies this as a gap in online boosting, despite existing statistical boosting methods for both settings.

The authors provide an online agnostic boosting algorithm that starts with a weak learner whose regret guarantee is only marginally better than trivial. It converts that learner into a strong one with sublinear regret. Sublinear regret means the cumulative shortfall against the comparison benchmark grows more slowly than the number of rounds, so the average shortfall diminishes.

The construction uses a simple abstract reduction to online convex optimization, allowing an arbitrary online convex optimizer to be converted efficiently into an online booster. The same reduction extends to statistical learning and to online realizable learning. Its significance is therefore both a new guarantee for agnostic online boosting and a shared framework covering the four combinations of statistical or online learning with agnostic or realizable assumptions.
neurips-2020-online-agnostic-boosting-vi.tldr: A reduction to online convex optimization turns weak regret guarantees into strong online agnostic boosting with sublinear regret.

paragraphs: Adversarial training seeks network parameters that perform well even under adversarial input perturbations. Although it often achieves low robust training loss in practice, explaining that success theoretically is difficult. Its min-max objective complicates the extension of convergence arguments developed for ordinary supervised training of highly over-parameterized neural networks.

This paper proves convergence to low robust training loss for ReLU networks with width polynomial in the input dimension, under assumptions described by the authors as natural. The earlier result discussed in the abstract required width exponential in that dimension and an unusual activation function. Replacing exponential width with polynomial width substantially improves the dimensional dependence of the theoretical requirement.

A key step shows that ReLU networks near their initialization can approximate a step function, supplying an ingredient for the convergence proof. The result helps explain optimization success in adversarial training within the stated theoretical setting. Its guarantee concerns low robust loss on the training data; that is the specific achievement established by the analysis, alongside the potentially useful approximation result near initialization.
neurips-2020-over-parameterized-adversar.tldr: Under stated assumptions, adversarial training of ReLU networks reaches low robust training loss with polynomial rather than exponential width.

paragraphs: Iterative hierarchical data augmentation, or IHDA, improves an already trained network by adding synthetic examples within its learned feature spaces. The motivation is that different layers capture different representations, and augmentation can be especially useful in regions the model finds difficult to classify. This makes the learned representation itself the setting for targeted augmentation.

At a chosen layer, IHDA transforms features into a distribution space and uses learned distributions to generate samples around difficult data points. It identifies those points by analyzing their neighborhoods. The synthetic samples fine-tune the following layers, after which the process moves to the next feature level. A dropout-probability mechanism is gradually relaxed toward higher-level feature spaces to address overfitting.

The paper reports state-of-the-art performance for several networks on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, exceeding existing augmentation approaches for the same networks. It also reports significant improvements on wearable-sensor activity recognition. These findings demonstrate the method in both image and non-image settings, supporting the usefulness of targeting difficult regions across a hierarchy of learned representations.
neurips-2020-post-training-iterative-hie.tldr: IHDA fine-tunes trained networks by synthesizing examples in difficult regions of successive feature spaces, improving tested image and sensor tasks.

paragraphs: Many machine learning models turn a vector of scores into probabilities before making predictions or computing a training objective. Such mappings can act as smooth approximations to choosing only the highest-scoring entry. A temperature-like parameter controls their behavior, and the abstract notes that its value can affect the quality of the resulting model.

Common approaches keep that parameter fixed or change it according to a shared schedule over training. Rankmax instead adapts it to each individual training example. The contribution is therefore an example-dependent probability mapping, allowing the approximation to the maximum-selection operation to vary across inputs instead of depending only on a global parameter choice.

The proposed method has sparse support, meaning some output probabilities can be exactly zero, and admits a numerically efficient implementation. The authors find that it can significantly outperform competing non-adaptive projection methods. These results support adapting the score-to-probability transformation as part of model design, with sparsity and efficient computation accompanying the reported empirical improvements.
neurips-2020-rankmax-an-adaptive-project.tldr: Rankmax adapts a temperature-like probability projection parameter per example, providing sparse outputs and reported gains over non-adaptive alternatives.

paragraphs: Value-based reinforcement learning requires choosing an action using an estimate of its value. When each action is a combinatorial object, the number of possibilities can make exhaustive comparison impractical. This paper develops a framework that makes action selection an explicit mixed-integer optimization problem, connecting a learned value function to a structured optimization procedure.

The application is the capacitated vehicle routing problem, where a single vehicle with limited capacity must cover a set of locations. The authors define each action as constructing an entire route. They use a deterministic policy and improve it through a simple policy iteration algorithm, with optimization handling the search over possible route actions.

On standard library instances of medium size, the approach is competitive with other reinforcement learning methods and has an average gap of 1.7% relative to state-of-the-art operations research methods. The result demonstrates a practical way to use value-based learning when actions are too numerous to enumerate. Its reported performance concerns the tested routing instances, where route construction provides the combinatorial decision structure.
neurips-2020-reinforcement-learning-with.tldr: Mixed-integer optimization enables value-based reinforcement learning to select whole routes from a combinatorial action space.

paragraphs: The ideal point model represents a user and candidate items in a common feature space. Its central assumption is that items closer to the user’s ideal point are more preferred. This paper revisits how closeness is defined, arguing that the usual Euclidean distance excludes interactions between features and the user’s underlying preferences.

The authors instead treat distance as an unknown Mahalanobis metric and learn it together with the user’s ideal point. Their evidence consists of paired comparisons stating that one item is preferred to another. This allows the method to infer both where the user’s preferred combination of features lies and how feature differences contribute to distance from that point.

The task can also be viewed as metric learning with some point locations unknown in advance. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the algorithm’s effectiveness. The contribution expands the flexibility of an ideal point representation while retaining its basic distance-based assumption: preference learning determines both the target location and the geometry used to compare items with that target.
neurips-2020-simultaneous-preference-and.tldr: Paired preference comparisons jointly identify a user’s ideal item and a distance metric that can capture feature interactions.

paragraphs: Submodular maximization selects a set whose value exhibits diminishing returns as elements are added. This paper considers a monotone objective under a combination of structural and budget constraints. It introduces a technique inspired by barrier functions in continuous optimization, using a potential function to connect constrained set selection with an approximate minimization problem.

The guarantee applies to a k-matchoid together with ell knapsack constraints, provided ell is no greater than k. Minimizing the proposed potential to within epsilon error guarantees a feasible solution with approximation factor 2(k+1+epsilon). An enumeration technique improves that factor to k+1+epsilon. These factors express a worst-case comparison with the optimal feasible objective value.

The authors state that the technique improves running time and provides a state-of-the-art guarantee. They also evaluate it across movie recommendation, summaries of YouTube videos and Twitter feeds, Yelp business locations, and a set cover problem. The main contribution is a reusable optimization connection: approximate minimization of a carefully constructed potential provides a route to feasible sets with explicit quality guarantees under combined constraints.
neurips-2020-submodular-maximization-thr.tldr: A barrier-inspired potential function yields improved runtime and approximation guarantees for submodular maximization under combined constraints.

paragraphs: Multiplayer online battle arena games challenge learning systems through multiple agents, large state and action spaces, and complex controls. This paper focuses on another scaling problem: expanding the available heroes creates a rapidly growing number of possible team lineups. An agent must cope with those combinations to handle a broader range of full-game play.

The authors propose a deep reinforcement learning paradigm that combines off-policy adaptation, multi-head value estimation, curriculum self-play, policy distillation, and Monte Carlo tree search. The combination is designed to support training and play with a large hero pool while addressing scalability. The contribution lies in coordinating these techniques into a system for the expanded lineup challenge.

The system is tested in Honor of Kings, where the authors demonstrate agents capable of defeating top esports players and describe their performance as superhuman. They also report a large-scale performance evaluation. These findings establish the approach’s effectiveness in the evaluated game, supporting progress toward broader MOBA play as hero diversity and possible agent combinations increase.
neurips-2020-towards-playing-full-moba-g.tldr: A combined reinforcement learning framework scales MOBA training to a large hero pool and defeats top esports players in Honor of Kings.

paragraphs: Transfer learning uses a model trained in one domain to help learning in another, often where data are scarce. Although widely used, the source of its benefits is not fully understood. This paper develops tools and analyses to distinguish what comes from reusing learned features from what comes from learning higher-level statistical properties of data.

The authors investigate transfer to images whose blocks have been shuffled. Through this analysis, they separate feature reuse from the effect of high-level data statistics and show that some transfer benefits arise from the latter. The finding broadens the explanation of successful transfer beyond a model simply carrying useful feature detectors from one task into another.

The paper also examines the optimization behavior of models initialized with pretrained weights. In the analyzed settings, training remains in the same basin of the loss landscape, and different resulting models are similar in feature space and close in parameter space. Together, these observations connect transfer benefits with both learned data statistics and the region of parameter space established by pretraining.
neurips-2020-what-is-being-transferred-i.tldr: Analyses of shuffled-image transfer show that some benefits come from high-level data statistics, alongside structure retained from pretrained initialization.
